name: Marcus Reyes, step-down: DKA with AKI on CKD G3b

caseMeta.title: Step-down / telemetry: type 1 diabetes in DKA with acute kidney injury on CKD G3b (repaired posterior urethral valves): cautious fluids, potassium that falls on insulin and is replaced one small bag at a time, crackles with low urine output, a low glucose after transition, mild rebound hyperkalemia (3 days, checkpoints at every 0700 and 1900)
learningObjectives: Manage an adult DKA protocol (2024 consensus) in a patient with AKI on CKD: small reassessed saline boluses, fixed-rate insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h with no bolus, dextrose and 0.05 unit/kg/h once glucose is under 250, hourly glucose, and the resolution criteria (BHB under 0.6 plus venous pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 or higher).

Apply the renal-modified peripheral potassium rule: never more than 10 mEq per hour from all sources, no potassium in the maintenance fluid, hold the insulin for K under 3.5 and replace by individually authorized one-bag riders only when the previous hour of urine is at least 40 mL (0.5 mL/kg/h), restart insulin only at K 3.5 or higher with prescriber confirmation; recognize why phosphate is monitored, not replaced.

Recognize fluid overload and low urine output early (fine crackles, 25 mL/h), count every IV volume, and respond without an automatic bolus or diuretic (D10W 50 mL/h, bladder scan, non-contrast ultrasound).

Carry out the transition with renal insulin-clearance caution (basal 2 hours before the drip stops), prevent and treat the low glucose that follows, recognize mild hyperkalemia with a normal-looking ECG, and teach sick-day insulin, kidney protection (held losartan, no NSAIDs, contrast caution, renal dosing) and teach-back to the patient and partner.

orders.name: Establish two peripheral IVs (right forearm 18 g, left forearm 20 g); no central line. Maintain patency; assess sites with each infusion check and at least hourly during irritant infusions. Insulin runs on its own dedicated pump and line; other fluids and intermittent potassium share the other line through a compatible connection. Saline flushes for line care are counted on the I&O: 20 mL per 12-hour shift through Day 3 0700, then 10 mL per shift. No uncounted maintenance or KVO carrier
orders.instructions: Never flush insulin-containing tubing into the patient or interrupt the dedicated insulin line for routine flushing: use the other IV for compatible medication and line care. After the insulin stops, disconnect and clear residual drug per policy before saline locking. Priming volume discarded before connection is not counted as intake.

orders.name: insulin regular (HUMULIN R) 100 units in 0.9% sodium chloride 100 mL (1 unit/mL) infusion - DKA (fixed rate)
orders.instructions: Regular insulin 100 units in NS to 100 mL (1 unit/mL) on a dedicated pump channel and line, 8 units/h to start, NO bolus. Independent two-nurse check of drug, concentration and rate at every bag and rate change. POC glucose hourly, including any hold; aim for an initial fall of 50-75 mg/dL per hour. If the fall is outside that range for two checks, or over 100 in one hour, call the prescriber to assess the pump, fluids, glucose and need for titration. Do NOT automatically raise the insulin during a potassium hold. At glucose under 250: add dextrose and reduce to 4 units/h. STOP/HOLD for K under 3.5, suspected severe hypoglycemia or urgent clinical deterioration and notify immediately; keep checking glucose and give individualized dextrose. Restart after K is 3.5 or higher WITH prescriber confirmation. Do not stop for gap closure alone. Final discontinuation needs the transition order and the basal overlap.
orders.rationale: K 5.8 (over 3.5) so insulin may start after the first 500 mL. 80 kg x 0.1 = 8 units/h; no bolus. When glucose falls under 250 add dextrose and lower to 0.05 unit/kg/h = 4 units/h; keep the insulin running until the ketones clear. Reduced kidney insulin clearance raises the later low-glucose risk.
nursingConsiderations: Hourly POC glucose; strict I&O; telemetry.
High-alert drug: two-nurse check of drug, concentration, rate and patient.
Stop only by order, after the first subcutaneous basal insulin dose has had its overlap.

medication.dose: 0.1 unit/kg/h = 8 units/h (8 mL/h); 0.05 unit/kg/h = 4 units/h (4 mL/h) once glucose is under 250
medication.importantInfo: Insulin stops ketone production; the acidosis (pH, bicarbonate, anion gap, beta-hydroxybutyrate) is the target, not the glucose. Insulin moves potassium into the cells: the blood potassium falls even though the body is low on potassium. With AKI the kidneys clear less insulin, so the effect lasts longer.
medication.freqKey: Continuous (adult DKA protocol)

orders.name: RENAL-MODIFIED POTASSIUM PROTOCOL: never more than 10 mEq/h from all sources; no 40 mEq/L bags; no potassium in maintenance fluids; HOLD insulin if K is under 3.5
orders.instructions: PERIPHERAL POTASSIUM SAFETY PROTOCOL FOR AKI ON CKD (two peripheral IVs, no central line): before ANY potassium, confirm the urine measured in the previous hour is at least 40 mL (0.5 mL/kg/h at 80 kg) and review the latest creatinine and ECG. TOTAL IV potassium from ALL sources across BOTH lines must NEVER exceed 10 mEq per hour. Never IV push. Never use a 40 mEq/L bag (central-line strength). No potassium is added to any maintenance fluid for this patient (a maintenance additive would be 20 mEq/L at most, and none is ordered). K 5.0 or higher, or any concerning ECG change = no potassium. K 3.5-4.9 = review the trend and urine output with the prescriber before any supplement; the usual target is 4-5; no automatic replacement in AKI. K UNDER 3.5 = HOLD the insulin infusion and notify the prescriber at once; if urine output is adequate and there is no ECG or other contraindication, give KCl 10 mEq in 100 mL premixed piggyback over 1 hour on a pump, ONE bag at a time (up to four in a row may be authorized, each by the current labs: it is never an automatic 40 mEq dose). Check K after each bag or at the ordered sampling time, from a site away from the infusing lines. Stop further replacement for falling urine output, K 4.0 or higher, a rising K, or an ECG concern pending prescriber review. Telemetry and IV-site assessment at least hourly during replacement. The 10 mEq/100 mL piggyback is a separate intermittent product, not a maintenance additive. No potassium phosphate substitution without a new order.
orders.rationale: Adult DKA protocol adapted to AKI on CKD G3b: potassium shifts into cells with insulin while the kidneys clear it poorly, so replacement is cautious, individually authorized and limited to 10 mEq/h through peripheral IVs.

orders.name: Initial labs (ED): BMP with calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, beta-hydroxybutyrate, venous blood gas, CBC, albumin, lactate, HbA1c, urinalysis, respiratory influenza / COVID PCR. Repeat BMP/Ca/Mg/phosphorus/BHB/VBG at 0400 and 0640; potassium-only draw at 0500 (two hours after insulin starts). Unit DKA panels at 1040, 1440 and 1840. Report BMP/VBG/BHB within 20 minutes and potassium-only within 10 minutes. No further DKA gases once resolution is confirmed
orders.instructions: Draw from an arm without an infusion running. DKA resolves only when BHB is under 0.6 AND venous pH is 7.3 or higher OR bicarbonate is 18 or higher (2024 consensus).

orders.name: Point-of-care glucose hourly while IV insulin is ordered, including any hold for potassium, until the infusion is discontinued
orders.instructions: Use the result for the insulin and dextrose steps (see the infusion order). Call for a fall over 100 mg/dL in one hour, a glucose under 150 while ketones persist, or any glucose under 70.

orders.name: Admit to step-down / telemetry (bed approved for IV insulin, continuous telemetry and hourly glucose checks): DKA after insulin omission during an acute illness, AKI on CKD G3b (congenital posterior urethral valve disease). Full Code

Continuous telemetry. Vital assessments every 2 hours during the insulin infusion and every 4 hours after it. Neurologic assessment hourly during the infusion, then every 4 hours. Lung assessment before and after each bolus, at least every 2 hours during IV fluids and with any symptom. Strict I&O: measure each void, hourly totals during the infusion, every 4 hours afterward. Daily standing weight at 0700 (same scale and clothing). NOTIFY for urine under 40 mL/h (0.5 mL/kg/h) for 2 hours, new crackles or dyspnea, rising oxygen need, mental change, arrhythmia or hemodynamic deterioration
orders.instructions: Consider ICU transfer if monitoring or treatment exceeds step-down capability. Peaked T = high K; flat T with U waves = low K, but a normal-looking tracing does not exclude a dangerous potassium level.

orders.name: Nephrology and endocrinology consultation today. Pharmacy medication and renal-dosing review today. Diabetes educator and dietitian Day 2. Case management Day 2. Each follows through discharge as needed
orders.instructions: Assisted bathroom and chair activity until reassessed.

orders.name: Assisted bathroom and chair activity; fall precautions (volume depletion, insulin infusion). Independent corridor walking from Day 2 1000 after a nursing safety check

HOLD home losartan (AKI, volume depletion, hyperkalemia risk). NO NSAIDs; avoid nonessential iodinated IV contrast and other nephrotoxins (if contrast becomes essential, the prescriber and nephrology assess benefit, risk and a protection plan). Pharmacy reviews every new renally cleared medicine using the changing kidney function, not the automatic eGFR alone. No routine bicarbonate, phosphate or magnesium replacement: assess for deficiency symptoms and repeat levels. Severe phosphate depletion or muscle, breathing or heart compromise needs urgent prescriber review and a separate renal-adjusted order
orders.instructions: The automatic eGFR reported with each panel is an estimate that is unreliable while creatinine is changing; it is not a measured GFR.

Count the volume on the I&O. Hold rapid-acting insulin during hypoglycemia and notify the prescriber. Basal insulin in type 1 diabetes is never permanently omitted: obtain a prescriber dose adjustment.

stickyNotes.title: Potassium: peripheral IVs, 10 mEq/h limit, AKI on CKD
stickyNotes.body: Two peripheral IVs, no central line. TOTAL potassium from ALL sources on BOTH lines never more than 10 mEq per hour. No 40 mEq/L bags and no potassium in any maintenance fluid. K under 3.5: HOLD insulin, call, then KCl 10 mEq/100 mL over 1 hour ONE bag at a time ONLY if the last hour of urine was at least 40 mL and the prescriber authorizes each bag. Check K after each bag. Peaked T = high K; flat T + U waves = low K; a normal tracing does not exclude either.

stickyNotes.title: Insulin infusion rules (80 kg)
stickyNotes.body: 8 units/h (0.1 unit/kg/h), no bolus. Glucose under 250: add dextrose AND lower to 4 units/h (0.05). Aim 150-200 while the ketones clear. Call: glucose under 150, a fall over 100 in 1 h, vomiting, confusion. DKA is over only with BHB under 0.6 AND (pH 7.3 or higher OR bicarbonate 18 or higher). Kidney disease prolongs insulin action: low glucose is the late risk.

stickyNotes.title: Kidney rules
stickyNotes.body: AKI on CKD G3b (baseline creatinine 2.0-2.2). Urine under 40 mL/h (0.5 mL/kg/h) for 2 hours = notify. No NSAIDs, avoid contrast, losartan on hold. The automatic eGFR is only an estimate while creatinine changes: do not dose from it alone. Count EVERY IV volume (riders, flushes, insulin carrier). No fluid bolus without a provider reassessment of lungs, perfusion and output.

stickyNotes.title: Insulin held for K 3.4
stickyNotes.body: Insulin infusion held at 1100. D5NS and hourly glucose continue. KCl 10 mEq/100 mL one bag at a time (urine OK, prescriber authorizes each); recheck K at 1150 and 1240 by separate venipuncture; restart only when K is 3.5 or higher AND the prescriber confirms.

notes.title: ED Provider Note - DKA with AKI on CKD
notes.author: W. Cole, MD
notes.summary: Type 1 diabetes and CKD G3b (repaired posterior urethral valves) with 3 days of illness and missed insulin. Glucose 620, bicarbonate 10, anion gap 25, venous pH 7.22, BHB 7.2, K 5.8, creatinine 3.4 (baseline about 2.1). notes.body:
**HPI**
31-year-old man with type 1 diabetes since age 9 and CKD G3b from posterior urethral valves repaired in infancy (baseline creatinine 2.0-2.2). Sore throat, myalgias, dry cough, nausea and poor intake began 11/02. He stopped his meal insulin when he stopped eating and skipped glargine on 11/03 and 11/04, believing all insulin requires food. Last evening he developed thirst, polyuria followed by less urine, diffuse abdominal discomfort and repeated nonbloody vomiting. He denies dysuria, flank pain, chest pain, toxic ingestion and NSAID use. His partner, Elena Cruz, brought him in.

**Exam**
Awake and oriented, dry mouth, deep respirations, lungs clear, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding or focal findings.

**Data (released 0220)**
Glucose 620, sodium 130 (corrected for glucose about 138), potassium 5.8, bicarbonate 10, anion gap 25, venous pH 7.22, BHB 7.2, BUN 64, creatinine 3.4 (known baseline near 2.1), phosphate 5.6, magnesium 2.1, lactate 1.5. The initial ECG shows no peaked T waves or QRS widening; a normal-looking tracing does not exclude hyperkalemia.

**Assessment and plan**
1. DKA (moderate by pH, severe by bicarbonate and ketones) from insulin omission during a presumed viral illness.
2. AKI on CKD G3b: creatinine is about 1.6 times baseline, stage 1 by the creatinine criterion. No known heart failure, anuria or dialysis history.
3. Volume: small 250 mL saline boluses with a lung and perfusion reassessment after each, not a standard large-volume sequence. Further boluses need provider reassessment.
4. Start IV regular insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/h (8 units/h at 80 kg) without a bolus after the first fluid; no potassium now (K 5.8), no bicarbonate (pH over 7.0). Repeat chemistry at 0400 and a potassium-only check at 0500.
5. Respiratory PCR sent; no focal bacterial source so far. Strict measured intake and output; continuous cardiac monitoring.

notes.body: Two peripheral IVs are patent (right forearm 18 gauge, left forearm 20 gauge) and the two 250 mL saline boluses are complete. Lung reassessments after each bolus remain clear. Regular insulin began at 0300 at 8 units per hour after an independent dose and pump check, on its own dedicated line; there was no insulin bolus. The 0300 bedside glucose was 600. Ondansetron 4 mg was given at 0225 for vomiting, with improvement in nausea since. The urinalysis has resulted with glucose and ketones but no evidence of infection, and every void is being measured.

notes.title: Step-Down Admission History and Physical
notes.author: I. Morgan, MD
notes.summary: DKA from insulin omission during a presumed viral illness, with stage 1 AKI on CKD G3b (congenital posterior urethral valves). 0700 panel: K 4.2 falling, bicarbonate 14, gap 18, BHB 4.8, creatinine 3.2, HbA1c 8.9%. Losartan held, nephrotoxins avoided, nephrology and endocrinology consulted, cautious fluids, no pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis (ambulatory, no clot-risk factor).
notes.body:
**Reason for admission**
Diabetic ketoacidosis triggered by insulin omission during an acute illness, with acute kidney injury on CKD G3b.

**HPI**
31-year-old man with type 1 diabetes since age 9 (one prior DKA at 22). Three days of sore throat, myalgias, dry cough, nausea and poor intake; he stopped meal insulin when he stopped eating and skipped glargine on 11/03 and 11/04 because he believed all insulin requires food. ED course: two 250 mL saline boluses, ondansetron once, regular insulin 8 units/h from 0300 without a bolus, saline 100 mL/h; no potassium given.

**Past history**
Congenital posterior urethral valves repaired in infancy with residual renal dysplasia and scarring: CKD G3b, baseline creatinine 2.0-2.2 (2.1 on 10/22), outpatient UACR 180 mg/g, followed by nephrology. Mild hypertension. No dialysis, transplant, catheter, heart failure, coronary or lung disease.

**Medications**
Glargine U-100 24 units nightly at 2100; lispro 1 unit per 12 g carbohydrate plus 1 unit per 50 mg/dL above 150 before meals (12-18 units/day); pens, CGM (sensor expired during the illness), no pump. Losartan 25 mg every morning; cholecalciferol 1,000 units daily. No SGLT2 inhibitor, metformin, potassium or phosphate product. **Allergies:** none known.

**Social / family**
Lives with his partner Elena Cruz; IT technician; insured, stable housing and food. Never smoked; occasional alcohol, none during illness; no recreational drugs. Father has hypertension, mother has hypothyroidism; no known familial kidney disease.

**Exam**
Alert, dry mouth, mild nausea, respirations still somewhat deep, lungs clear, no edema, two peripheral IVs, no central line. Telemetry shows sinus rhythm.

**Data (0700 release of the 0640 panel)**
Glucose 380, sodium 135, potassium 4.2, chloride 103, bicarbonate 14, anion gap 18, venous pH 7.29, BHB 4.8, BUN 59, creatinine 3.2, phosphate 3.8, magnesium 1.9. Admission HbA1c 8.9%. Point-of-care glucose 360.

**Assessment and plan**
1. **DKA, improving, not resolved.** Continue regular insulin 8 units/h and saline 100 mL/h, hourly glucose. When glucose falls under 250, add dextrose and reduce insulin to 4 units/h.
2. **Potassium is falling** (5.8, 5.0, 4.7, 4.2): add a panel at 0840. Insulin is held if K is under 3.5. Peripheral IVs only: potassium never above 10 mEq per hour from all sources, individually authorized in AKI.
3. **AKI on CKD G3b, stage 1 by the creatinine criterion** (3.2-3.4 is about 1.5-1.6 times baseline): reassess volume by examination, urine output and daily weights rather than a standard large-volume sequence. Hold losartan, no NSAIDs, avoid nonessential contrast. Nephrology and endocrinology consulted; pharmacy renal-dosing review. The automatic eGFR is not a measured GFR and is not used alone for dosing.
4. **Phosphate** 3.8 and falling with treatment: monitor with each panel; replace only for a value under 1.0 or muscle, breathing or heart problems.
5. **VTE risk:** young, ambulatory, no prior clot or other documented risk factor (CKD alone is not one); no pharmacologic prophylaxis. Reassess if he becomes immobile.
6. Assisted bathroom activity, fall precautions, telemetry, strict I&O with every void measured.

notes.title: Pharmacy Medication and Renal Dosing Review
notes.author: N. Gallagher, PharmD
notes.summary: Home medicines reconciled. Losartan held for AKI and hyperkalemia risk. Automatic eGFR is unreliable while creatinine changes: do not dose from it alone. Reduced kidney insulin clearance raises later hypoglycemia risk. Potassium only by one-bag riders, 10 mEq/h maximum. No pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis ordered (ambulatory, no risk factor).
notes.body:
Home doses were confirmed with the patient and his partner: glargine 24 units nightly, carbohydrate-based lispro with a correction factor, losartan 25 mg each morning and cholecalciferol 1,000 units daily. Losartan is appropriately held during the acute kidney injury and potassium disturbance.

The current creatinine is changing, so the automatic eGFR (24-26 so far) is only an estimate and should not be used alone to choose drug doses; I will review each new renally cleared medicine against the current creatinine, urine output and trend. The one ondansetron dose needs no renal adjustment, and I see no scheduled repeat. I verified the regular insulin concentration (100 units in 100 mL, 1 unit/mL) and the premixed potassium chloride 10 mEq/100 mL piggyback in the renal-modified protocol: one bag at a time, never above 10 mEq per hour from all sources, none in the maintenance fluid.

Reduced kidney clearance of insulin may increase hypoglycemia risk during and after the transition, so subcutaneous doses will need reassessment rather than an automatic return to the home regimen. He is young, ambulatory and has no clot history or other documented risk factor, so no pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis is ordered; I agree and will reassess if he becomes immobile. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and nonessential iodinated contrast are to be avoided.

Under the order written at 0900, normal saline is replaced by D5/0.9% saline at 100 mL/h with no added potassium and regular insulin is reduced to 4 units/h (0.05 unit/kg/h); it keeps running because the ketones are not cleared.

Potassium has fallen from 5.8 to 3.6 in about seven hours on insulin. It is above the insulin-hold threshold of 3.5, hourly urine is 50 mL (0.6 mL/kg/h) and creatinine is 3.3; with AKI I am not starting potassium on a single value, and I will review the trend with the next panel at 1040. If K is under 3.5 the insulin is held and replacement is given by individually authorized one-bag riders at no more than 10 mEq per hour. Lungs are clear and there is no edema at this assessment. Every IV volume continues to be counted.

notes.title: Nephrology Initial Consultation
notes.author: D. Lin, MD
notes.summary: CKD G3b from congenital posterior urethral valve disease (baseline creatinine about 2.1) with AKI most consistent with reduced renal perfusion; creatinine 3.3, K 3.6. No indication for kidney replacement therapy. Cautious fluids, frequent lung checks, strict urine measurement, daily weights, individualized potassium; hold losartan, avoid NSAIDs and contrast.
notes.body:
Marcus has established CKD G3b from congenital posterior urethral valve disease with a baseline creatinine near 2.1. The current AKI is most consistent with reduced renal perfusion during vomiting and osmotic losses, with possible evolving tubular injury. Creatinine on the latest available panel is 3.3 and potassium has fallen to 3.6 during DKA treatment.

He has no current indication for kidney replacement therapy and no history of anuria or dialysis dependence. Continue cautious fluids, frequent lung assessment, strict urine measurement, daily weights, and individualized potassium replacement after reviewing urine output; no automatic replacement. Hold losartan and avoid nonessential contrast and NSAIDs while monitoring for either congestion or persistent hypoperfusion. A creatinine that is still rising after volume repletion would prompt imaging of the repaired urinary tract.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Note - Low Potassium, Insulin Held
notes.author: I. Morgan, MD
notes.summary: 1100 results: K 3.4 (below 3.5), glucose 195, BHB 2.4, pH 7.32, bicarbonate 16, gap 15, phosphate 2.2, creatinine 3.4. Insulin held under protocol; one KCl 10 mEq/100 mL bag at 100 mL/h (previous hour urine 50 mL); D5NS and hourly glucose continue. ECG: mild T-wave flattening. Recheck K at 1150.
notes.body:
The 1040 specimen, released at 1100, shows potassium 3.4, glucose 195, bicarbonate 16, anion gap 15, venous pH 7.32, BHB 2.4, phosphate 2.2, magnesium 1.8 and creatinine 3.4. The bedside glucose at 1100 is 190. Potassium is under 3.5, so the insulin infusion is held under the potassium order. The pH is above 7.3 but BHB is 2.4, so ketoacidosis is not resolved and the hold is expected to be short.

The urine measured in the previous hour is 50 mL, above the 40 mL/h threshold, and there is no ECG contraindication; one KCl 10 mEq in 100 mL bag runs at 100 mL/h from 1100 with no other potassium source (10 mEq per hour maximum). D5NS continues and hourly glucose checks continue during the pause. The 12-lead ECG released at 1110 shows mild T-wave flattening without ectopy. A potassium-only specimen will be drawn at 1150 by separate venipuncture, and I will review it and the hour of urine before authorizing any second bag.

Phosphate 2.2 is being monitored; replacement is reserved for a value under 1.0 or muscle, breathing or heart compromise, and potassium phosphate would add to the potassium load in AKI. Magnesium 1.8 needs no replacement.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Note - Potassium Reassessment
notes.author: I. Morgan, MD
notes.summary: K 3.5 after the first 10 mEq bag; preceding hourly urine 50 mL; second KCl bag authorized 1200-1300. Insulin stays held: a K exactly at the threshold after one bag is not a confirmed restart value; decision after the 1240 panel. POC glucose 210 on D5NS.
notes.body:
The potassium-only specimen released at 1200 is 3.5 after the first KCl bag. The preceding hourly urine output is 50 mL, there is no IV-site pain or swelling, and the ECG showed only mild T-wave flattening. I authorized a second KCl 10 mEq/100 mL bag over one hour with no overlap, still no more than 10 mEq per hour from all sources; no third or fourth bag is ordered.

Insulin stays held. The restart rule is K 3.5 or higher with my confirmation, and a value exactly at the threshold, up only 0.1 after 10 mEq on a falling trend in AKI, is not a value I will confirm; I will decide on the 1240 panel, which results at 1300. The 1200 bedside glucose is 210 and dextrose support continues with hourly checks. I also want a fresh lung and urine assessment at 1300 because the fluid total now includes the potassium bags.

notes.title: Nephrology Follow-Up - Low Output and Lung Findings
notes.author: D. Lin, MD
notes.summary: 1300 panel: K 3.8, creatinine 3.5, bicarbonate 17, BHB 1.8. Fine basal crackles and a urine hour of 25 mL; bladder scan 70 mL. D5NS changed to D10W 50 mL/h (same 5 g/h dextrose, half the volume), insulin restarted at 4 units/h; no automatic bolus or diuretic; non-contrast ultrasound ordered.
notes.body:
The 1300 panel shows potassium 3.8, creatinine 3.5, bicarbonate 17 and BHB 1.8. Two cautious potassium bags are complete and no further potassium is ordered. The most recent urine hour (1200-1300) is 25 mL, below 0.5 mL/kg/h, and fine crackles have appeared at the lung bases without overt respiratory distress. The bladder scan at 1310 is 70 mL, so major retention is unlikely; a non-contrast renal and bladder ultrasound is ordered because of his urologic history.

We are reducing the dextrose-containing fluid volume by changing D5NS to D10W at 50 mL/h while keeping the same hourly glucose delivery, and restarting insulin at the ordered reduced rate now that K is 3.8. Do not give an automatic saline bolus or a diuretic solely for the creatinine value; reassess congestion, perfusion, output and the pending imaging, and watch the sodium with the free water in D10W. If urine stays under 40 mL/h for a second hour, that formally meets the notification threshold at 1400.

notes.title: Renal and Bladder Ultrasound Without Contrast
notes.author: Radiology Service (L. Brandt, MD)
notes.summary: Bilateral chronic renal scarring. No hydronephrosis, no acute obstruction. Bladder without significant retention.
notes.body:
**Exam**
Renal and bladder ultrasound, performed 1400. No contrast.

**Indication**
31-year-old with repaired congenital posterior urethral valves, CKD G3b and acute kidney injury; falling urine output at 1200-1300. Bladder scan 70 mL at 1310.

**Comparison**
None available.

**Findings**
- Both kidneys show chronic parenchymal scarring with cortical thinning.
- No hydronephrosis in either kidney. No calculi seen. No perinephric collection.
- Urinary bladder without significant retained urine.

**Impression**
Bilateral chronic renal scarring, consistent with the known history. No hydronephrosis or acute obstruction.

notes.title: Endocrinology Consult - DKA Reassessment
notes.author: G. Tran, MD
notes.summary: 1500 panel: glucose 203, K 4.3, bicarbonate 18, gap 12, pH 7.35 but BHB 1.0: not resolved by the ketone requirement. Continue insulin 4 units/h with low-volume dextrose and hourly glucose. Ultrasound: chronic scarring, no obstruction. No phosphate replacement (1.7, no symptoms). Plan a reduced, overlapped basal-bolus regimen.
notes.body:
The latest chemistry shows glucose 203, potassium 4.3, bicarbonate 18, anion gap 12 and venous pH 7.35. BHB remains 1.0, so ketoacidosis is not yet resolved by the consensus ketone requirement (BHB under 0.6 plus pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 or higher). The gap and the improving pH should not trigger premature discontinuation of insulin.

Continue regular insulin at 4 units/h with low-volume dextrose support and hourly bedside glucose assessment. The renal ultrasound has resulted with chronic scarring and no acute obstruction. Phosphate is 1.7 without weakness or cardiopulmonary compromise, so I see no reason to add phosphate. Calcium 8.4 with a normal admission albumin is asymptomatic: monitor, no replacement. Once ketones clear and oral intake is reliable, use a reduced basal-bolus plan with a documented overlap rather than restoring his full home regimen, because kidney insulin clearance is reduced and the requirement is likely lower.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Note - DKA Resolved, Transition
notes.author: I. Morgan, MD
notes.summary: 1900 results: BHB 0.4, pH 7.38, bicarbonate 21, gap 9, glucose 180: DKA resolved. notes.body:

Glargine 18 units (reduced from his home 24) is ordered for 1900 with an initial lispro dose of 3 units for the meal; the IV insulin and D10W continue until 2100 for a two-hour overlap and then stop if he is stable, not vomiting and has eaten. Lung findings have improved after the fluid volume was reduced, and the last hourly urine output is 50 mL. Continue renal surveillance and overnight glucose checks, because acute illness, reduced intake and impaired kidney function can make the subcutaneous insulin requirement lower than at home.

notes.body:

He was awake with a safe swallow, so he received 120 mL of apple juice (15 g carbohydrate) under the hypoglycemia order, and I was notified. The 0700 recheck is 92 with resolution of symptoms, and a solid carbohydrate and protein snack is being provided. The serum glucose of 62 released at 0700 was drawn at 0640, before treatment, and does not represent failure of the oral rescue.

His 0200 glucose was 108 and no correction insulin was given overnight. The likely contributors are glargine 18 units, the 3-unit meal dose and the 1-unit bedtime correction in a patient whose kidneys clear insulin more slowly. The morning panel shows BHB 0.3 (no recurrent ketosis), potassium 4.8, bicarbonate 22 and creatinine 3.0. Endocrinology will review the glargine, meal and correction doses this morning; basal insulin is not omitted in type 1 diabetes. Standing weight at 0700 is 81.0 kg, up 0.5 kg from arrival, with clear lungs.

notes.title: Endocrinology Dose Revision After Low Glucose
notes.author: G. Tran, MD
notes.summary: Symptomatic low glucose after the first transition night, treated orally. 0730 glucose 106; no recurrent ketosis; creatinine 3.0. At 0715: glargine reduced to 14 units at 1900, meal lispro 2 units immediately after a verified meal, bedtime correction discontinued. Basal insulin continues.
notes.body:
The overnight transition was followed by symptomatic hypoglycemia that responded to oral carbohydrate. The 0730 bedside glucose is 106, and there is no recurrent nausea or evidence of recurrent ketosis on the morning panel. Creatinine remains elevated at 3.0, with reduced intake and impaired renal insulin clearance contributing to a lower requirement.

At 0715 I reduced the next glargine dose to 14 units at 1900, changed meal lispro to 2 units immediately after a verified meal, and discontinued bedtime correction. Continue the conservative correction scale before meals only, with the specified spacing and no meal component when the meal is skipped. Basal insulin remains necessary in type 1 diabetes, and additional overnight checks will assess the revised regimen.

notes.title: Nephrology Follow-Up - Recovery Reassessment
notes.author: D. Lin, MD
notes.summary: Creatinine 3.0 and K 4.8 on the morning panel. Urine recovered overnight and lungs are clear without a diuretic. The six-hour low-output interval yesterday (about 0.3 mL/kg/h) and the creatinine ratio are consistent with stage 1 AKI; no dialysis indication. Weight up 0.5 kg. Oral fluids in divided amounts; losartan stays held.
notes.body:
Creatinine has decreased to 3.0 and potassium is 4.8 on the morning panel. Urine output recovered overnight and the lungs are clear without diuretic treatment. The six-hour low-output interval yesterday (25 mL per hour, about 0.3 mL/kg/h, from 1200 to 1800) and the peak creatinine of 3.5 against a baseline of 2.1 are consistent with stage 1 AKI, with no current dialysis indication.

Standing weight has risen modestly from unit arrival, reinforcing that examination and urine output should guide further fluid decisions. Continue oral fluids in divided amounts, strict balance records and daily weights rather than routine IV maintenance. Losartan remains held until kidney function and potassium are reassessed, and the discharge plan must clearly assign who decides on the restart.

notes.title: Diabetes Education - Initial Teaching
notes.author: E. Marchetti, RN, CDCES
notes.summary: He stopped all insulin because he was not eating and feared a low. Reviewed basal vs mealtime insulin; he can state that illness may need insulin even with little intake, with clinician-directed dose changes. Practiced the backup meter, blood ketone testing and the 15 g rule using this morning's low. Partner taking part.
notes.body: Marcus describes stopping all insulin because he was not eating and feared a low glucose. We reviewed the different purposes of continuous basal insulin and food-related rapid-acting insulin. He can now explain that illness may require insulin even when food intake is reduced, with clinician-directed dose adjustment rather than complete omission. We practiced checking glucose with the backup meter and reviewed blood ketone testing for illness or persistent hyperglycemia. The morning low-glucose episode was used to practice the 15 g treatment and 15-minute recheck process. His partner participated with his permission and will help locate ketone supplies and contact information before discharge.

notes.title: Renal Dietitian Nutrition Assessment

K 4.8 and phosphorus 2.2: no blanket potassium or phosphorus restriction; avoid potassium-based salt substitutes. Practiced carbohydrate estimation; fluids divided through the day.
notes.body:
Appetite is improving but remains below the patient's usual intake. The current plan uses consistent-carbohydrate meals, sodium reduction, and avoidance of high-protein supplements while AKI recovers. Potassium is 4.8 and phosphorus is 2.2 on the available morning results, so a blanket severe potassium and phosphorus restriction is not appropriate today. We discussed avoiding potassium-based salt substitutes and choosing minimally processed foods without imposing unnecessary limits.

He practiced estimating meal carbohydrate and identifying when a smaller meal requires individualized insulin guidance. Oral fluid intake will be divided through the day and adjusted with the team according to urine, weight and lung findings.

notes.title: Pharmacy Transition Review
notes.author: N. Gallagher, PharmD
notes.summary: Revised glargine, meal and correction orders are active; bedtime correction removed. Premeal glucose 112 and 174 needed no correction; intake was verified before each reduced lispro dose. Kidney impairment prolongs insulin action, so corrections are not repeated within 4 hours. Losartan on hold; no potassium or phosphate supplement. Apple juice or glucose tablets (not orange juice) for lows.
notes.body:
The revised basal and meal orders are active and the bedtime correction has been removed. The breakfast and lunch premeal bedside values are 112 and 174, and neither requires correction. Meal intake was verified before each reduced lispro dose was administered. We reviewed how reduced kidney function can prolong insulin action and why repeating correction doses too soon can cause hypoglycemia.

Losartan remains on hold and there is no ongoing potassium or phosphate replacement order. Because his potassium has swung both low and high, apple juice or glucose tablets are preferred over orange juice when treating a low. I will reconcile the final prescriptions against the current regimen and make sure he does not resume the previous 24-unit basal dose from an older medication list.

notes.body:

notes.body:
